content_items.title: Sustainability and collaboration in a time of uncertainty

programme.title: Sustainability and collaboration in a time of uncertainty
programme.session: SYM38 Sustaining the Geo- and Biodiversity Data Ecosystem: Standards-Driven Approaches to Long-Term Resilience
programme.abstract:
Over the past several decades, geo-and biodiversity sciences have been reshaped by digitization, data mobilization, and data integration efforts, giving rise to the community-developed Digital Extended Specimen as a unifying framework. These initiatives have produced substantial infrastructure, new tools and workflows, and a more connected global community. However, as funding cycles conclude, urgent challenges remain, including sustaining social, physical, and digital infrastructure; maintaining and aligning software and data quality work across networks; retaining expertise; coordinating governance; and supporting workforce development.

This presentation frames geo-and biodiversity data infrastructure as a distributed socio-technical system in which semantically structured and linked data, standards development, and data harmonization enable coordination, reduce duplication, and support research. It emphasizes that achieving machine-actionable, FAIR-and CARE-compliant data depends on sustaining a standards-based ecosystem of data providers, aggregators, platforms, repositories, and users.

Drawing on current efforts within the networks of the International Partners for the Digital Extended Specimen and the Biodiversity Collections Network, along with the broader community, this talk explores how coordinated approaches and research-and machine-ready standards can better align social, physical, and digital infrastructures needed to support community goals. It highlights opportunities to leverage economies of scale, strengthen governance and collaboration, and expand the relevance of biodiversity data across domains, offering a forward-looking perspective on building a more sustainable and integrated data ecosystem.

content_items.summary: Libby Ellwood introduced the International Partners for the Digital Extended Specimen (IPDES) and framed the symposium around sustaining the biodiversity data ecosystem. She presented the Digital Extended Specimen as a unifying architecture and identified three sustainability needs: technology and infrastructure, people, and funding. She argued that sustainability will come from a diverse, resilient funding portfolio rather than a single replacement source, and described how IPDES is taking this session to several conferences before synthesising the outcomes in a webinar.

content_items.title: GBIF after 25 years

programme.title: GBIF after 25 years
programme.session: SYM38 Sustaining the Geo- and Biodiversity Data Ecosystem: Standards-Driven Approaches to Long-Term Resilience
programme.abstract: This year GBIF celebrates its first 25 years. GBIF has grown from a big idea to a highly productive global network and biodiversity infrastructure. GBIF originated from the natural history museum community as an infrastructure to share data from specimens. GBIF now mediates data from over 285 million specimens and GRSciColl contains information from nearly 11,000 collections around the world. This success is due to the global GBIF network of over 2,600 data publishers and national nodes. The integration of data from different sources allows connection to related data with images, DNA sequences and even phylogenies. This data sharing allows reuse for many scientific applications beyond taxonomy and systematics such as conservation, invasive species research and climate change. At GBIF we track data usage and confirm the use of collection data in strategic documents that inform policy such as the IPBES assessment on invasive species. GBIF users link their GBIF-enabled research to achieving UN Sustainable Development Goals. Perhaps most importantly the easy access to shared digitized data is immediately available to national reporting and the CBD Global Biodiversity Framework. GBIF has succeeded by providing needed support for the nations that require. GBIF sustainability has benefited by its unique governance structure and community engagement. This collaboration will be even more important as move forward together for the next 25 years.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced by the chair as Joe Miller; content on GBIF's 25th year matches the programme. Chair thanks 'Joe and Fede' afterwards, suggesting a colleague (Fede) was credited.

content_items.summary: Joe Miller explained how the GBIF Secretariat approaches sustainability: stable GDP-based national contributions from about 40 member countries, leveraged with European Commission grants, foundations and special funds so the budget has doubled in five years. He described DOI-based citation tracking showing data reuse in science and policy, and how about a quarter of the budget flows back out through BID and CESP programmes. He emphasised aligning with policy and funding mechanisms such as the CBD, GEF 9 and the Global Biodiversity Framework Fund, and previewed a pilot indexing South African data with the national taxonomy.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: GBIF sustains itself by leveraging stable national contributions into additional funding and by embedding itself in the biodiversity policy and funding architecture.
content_items.why_it_matters: It offers a concrete, working model of how a global biodiversity infrastructure demonstrates value and secures long-term funding, including the policy links now being built with CBD and GEF.

DOIs on downloads allow tracking of data use; about eight peer-reviewed publications per day use GBIF-mediated data.
31 of 32 key messages of the 2023 IPBES invasive alien species assessment drew on literature using GBIF-mediated data.
Contributions are GDP-based under a five-year MoU; leveraging this stability, the overall budget has doubled, giving roughly two euros of work programme per euro contributed.
About 25% of the budget goes out to BID, CESP projects and contractors around the world.
GBIF is working with the CBD, GEF, World Bank and UNDP; the CBD Executive Secretary encouraged all parties to join GBIF.
Two thirds of seventh national reports to the CBD mention GBIF, but there are disconnects between national focal points.
A pilot indexes South African botanical data against South Africa's own national taxonomy, to be shown at COP17.

content_items.title: Unifying Natural Heritage for a Resilient Future

programme.title: Unifying Natural Heritage for a Resilient Future
programme.session: SYM38 Sustaining the Geo- and Biodiversity Data Ecosystem: Standards-Driven Approaches to Long-Term Resilience
programme.abstract:
In an era defined by rapid environmental shifts and global instability, the mobilization of biodiversity data is no longer a luxury-it is a necessity for informed survival. DiSSCo (Distributed System of Scientific Collections) represents a transformative response to this uncertainty, transitioning fragmented physical collections with specimens into a synchronized, FAIR-compliant digital ecosystem built on the Digital Extended Specimen concept.

This presentation explores how DiSSCo fosters collaboration by unifying over 1.5 billion biological and geological objects across hundreds of institutions. At the heart of this infrastructure is the open Digital Specimen, using a FAIR Digital Object compliant architecture that enables researchers and collection curators to link, analyze, and enrich collection data with the help of machines at an unprecedented scale.

By harmonizing institutional efforts, DiSSCo ensures the long-term sustainability of scientific assets, providing the evidentiary base required to tackle climate change, biodiversity loss, and emerging health risks. We will discuss the technical and organizational frameworks that allow DiSSCo to bridge the gap between isolated silos and a shared knowledge base. Ultimately, DiSSCo demonstrates that through integrated digital infrastructure and collaborative governance, natural heritage can pivot from a state of fragmented, fragile silos to a future of data-driven resilience.

actual.identification_notes: Chair's introduction is garbled by ASR as 'Dr. Adrian'; chair thanks 'Wouter' afterwards and content is on DiSSCo, matching the programme.

content_items.summary: Wouter Addink used Shackleton's Endurance expedition as a parable of resilience (acting immediately and protecting the most precious assets) before presenting DiSSCo. He explained that only about 10% of Europe's estimated 1.5 billion specimens are digitised, and that DiSSCo aims to industrialise digitisation and create one FAIR, machine-actionable European virtual collection built around the Digital Extended Specimen as a citable FAIR digital object with a DOI. He argued that the ERIC legal model, with member-state financial and governance commitments, frees data from project-cycle dependency.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: DiSSCo's ERIC model and FAIR digital specimen objects are intended to make Europe's specimen data resilient beyond short-term project funding.
content_items.why_it_matters: Specimens provide evidence for biodiversity loss, climate change and health research, and a long-term legal and funding structure is presented as the answer to data loss when project funding ends.
key_points: Resilience means taking immediate action and focusing on preserving the most precious assets, illustrated by Shackleton's expedition.
Specimens are evidence for biodiversity loss, climate adaptation and pathogen/health research.
Only about 10% of an estimated 1.5 billion European specimens are digitised.
The DiSSCo digital specimen is a FAIR digital object with a DOI, containing catalogue data and links to derived and related data.
The ERIC model provides long-term governance and financial commitments from member states, beyond project-cycle dependency.
DiSSCo has submitted its step-two ERIC application, with six founding countries, aiming to launch next year; over 400 institutions from 23 countries are involved.

notable_claims.claim: Only about 10% of Europe's estimated 1.5 billion specimens are currently digitised.
DiSSCo has submitted its step-two ERIC application with six founding member countries and hopes to launch the ERIC next year.
More than 400 institutions from 23 countries are involved in DiSSCo.

future_work: Launch of the DiSSCo ERIC, with more countries expected to join.
examples_case_studies: Shackleton's Endurance expedition as a resilience analogy.

representative_excerpt.text: Resilience is not about avoiding that crash that happens, but it is about taking immediate action.

notable_moments.description: Link from the Shackleton story to resilience of the community's assets.
The DiSSCo digital specimen as an actionable, citable FAIR digital object.

content_items.title: Requirements of Sustainability Models for Geo-Biodiversity Data Cyberinfrastructure

programme.title: Requirements of Sustainability Models for Geo-Biodiversity Data Cyberinfrastructure
programme.session: SYM38 Sustaining the Geo- and Biodiversity Data Ecosystem: Standards-Driven Approaches to Long-Term Resilience
programme.abstract:
The sustainability of cyberinfrastructure (CI) for Geo-Biodiversity (GB) research depends on the existence of a sustainable GB community of entities (aka ecosystem) which includes data providers, data aggregators, users, professional organizations and others. Conversely, a healthy progressive GB ecosystem also needs a sustainable CI for its own sustainability. This interdependence originates significant CI requirements which fall into three categories, namely, functional requirements, operational requirements and economic-model requirements. Functional requirements relate to the research activities that the CI must support such as biodiversity data management, data analytics, FAIROS practices, educational tools and workforce training. Operational requirements follow from the need for efficiency, scalability, security and resiliency of CI services. Economic-model requirements relate to tracking usage of resources (including data) and associated costs, generation and allocation of revenue, and accounting to funding sources and stakeholders.

This presentation reviews the possible funding models for scientific CI in the context of the GB ecosystem and discusses the CI features that they require, elaborating on the nature of these requirements and possible solutions. These requirements need to be addressed in the context of existing software , design patterns and data standards for economic activities in cyberspace. While paid commercial solutions are provided, open-source solutions that can be adopted and integrated with relevant standards are also possible. This presentation will also provide an example of how a prototype agentic system for biodiversity data exploration, integration and analytics, called iChatBio, could be extended to address some of these requirements.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced by the chair as Jose Fortes; he describes himself as a cyberinfrastructure designer working with IPDES and iDigBio. Affiliation inferred from iDigBio/ChatBio context.

content_items.summary: José Fortes asked how cyberinfrastructure design changes when sustainability is a first-order requirement, using music streaming (radio to Spotify) as an ecosystem in which aggregators and distributors route revenue back to content creators. He argued that biodiversity funding will become a hybrid of central grants, subscriptions, pay-as-you-go and partnerships, while stressing he supports open, free data for science. Because every model requires reporting use, cyberinfrastructure must add 'economic orchestration' (tracking who uses what, charging and distributing revenue), which needs community standards; ChatBio's usage tracking was offered as an early example.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Cyberinfrastructure sustainability and ecosystem sustainability go hand in hand, so infrastructure must be designed from the start to track use and support economic orchestration.
content_items.why_it_matters: It reframes sustainability as a design requirement for infrastructure and raises open questions about what the community would charge for and how revenue could reach small providers.
key_points: Sustaining infrastructure is only possible if the ecosystem of providers and users is sustainable, and vice versa.
Funding is shifting from funders distinct from users towards hybrids including subscriptions, advertising, pay-as-you-go and industry partnerships.
All models require reporting of use, so infrastructure must track use of data and services and how revenue is distributed.
Beyond technical orchestration, cyberinfrastructure needs an economic orchestration component; TDWG-style standards would be needed for it.
Open questions include what to charge for: records, images, bytes or services.
Small providers cannot build this themselves and need ways to interface with the ecosystem.
ChatBio uses agents to access multiple resources and tracks which data sources were used, by whom, per session.
questions: What should the biodiversity community charge for: records, images, bytes or services?
How should revenue be distributed across providers to ensure sustainability?

notable_claims.claim: Cyberinfrastructure sustainability is the same as ecosystem sustainability; they go hand in hand.
Future infrastructure funding will be hybrids of centralised funding and customer-based funding rather than a one-way trend.

recommendations: Design infrastructure to track everything done, who does what and for what purpose.
Foster collaboration between the biodiversity community and the cyberinfrastructure community on economic models.
examples_case_studies: Music streaming ecosystem as an analogy.
ChatBio session-level resource tracking.

q_and_a.question: Andre Zerger (Atlas of Living Australia) asked, in the later discussion, whether there are exemplars of such models in adjacent domains.
q_and_a.answer_summary: Fortes said no; the music economy was the most relatable example he found and he would take the question away.

representative_excerpt.text: So, you can think of the big question being, how does the biodiversity ecosystem economy work, and how does the cyberinfrastructure support it?

notable_moments.description: The music streaming ecosystem analogy.
Economic orchestration as a new cyberinfrastructure component.
ChatBio usage tracking example.

content_items.title: From preservation to perseverance: bridging disciplines for data resilience

programme.title: From preservation to perseverance: bridging disciplines for data resilience
programme.session: SYM38 Sustaining the Geo- and Biodiversity Data Ecosystem: Standards-Driven Approaches to Long-Term Resilience
programme.abstract:
Since 2025, major federal funding cuts in the US have put multiple scientific data infrastructures at risk, including many in the Earth and environmental sciences. For example, multiple data resources managed by NOAA, USGS and other federal agencies have been taken offline, typically without plans for replacement or restoration. Many NASA science programs have been cut, and multiple NSF programs for research and infrastructure in the Earth sciences are canceled or rumored to be canceled. The funding programs that remain are increasingly skewed toward AI and partnerships with industry. Earth science data infrastructures are having to quickly pivot to alternative funding models, and are discussing worst case scenarios in case of closure.

The Earth and biodiversity sciences have much to gain from coordination and partnership in this increasingly uncertain funding landscape. In this talk, I’ll share sustainability efforts taken by data infrastructures in the Earth and environmental sciences, including the System for Earth and Extraterrestrial Sample Registration (SESAR), which include diversifying our funding streams and refactoring our codebase and vocabularies. I’ll also discuss broader resilience efforts in the US-based Earth science community, including nascent community-building initiatives from the American Geophysical Union. I’ll conclude by reflecting on existing digital preservation insights from scholars in the library and information sciences, and how these present us with important guidance as we seek to persevere through times of uncertainty and resource scarcity.

actual.identification_notes: Pre-recorded video, introduced by the chair; speaker self-identifies. The first seconds of the video were accidentally replayed afterwards (01:11:22).

content_items.summary: Andrea Thomer described how Earth science data infrastructures in the US moved from the passive threat of invisibility to active threats in 2025, when NOAA and other agency resources were taken offline and many staff lost their jobs. She presented three resilience efforts at different timescales: SESAR rescuing NOAA's Index to Marine and Lacustrine Geological Samples (IMLGS), the ESIP Repository Crisis Scorecards for self-assessment against four crisis scenarios, and an AGU-led, Hewlett-funded international initiative building roadmaps, business models and mutual aid networks. She concluded that resilience is about prioritisation, doing the best with what we have, and called for advocacy to keep infrastructure appropriately visible.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Data resilience in a crisis is about prioritisation and mutual aid rather than perfection, and infrastructures need to be kept appropriately visible to be funded.
content_items.why_it_matters: The Earth science community's experience of sudden defunding offers biodiversity informatics tested approaches (data rescue, crisis scorecards, mutual aid) and an invitation to collaborate.
key_points: Infrastructure is invisible by design (Bowker and Star) and only noticed when it breaks, which makes maintenance hard to fund.
In 2025 over 20 NOAA databases and data resources were taken offline after US federal budget cuts; half of her ESIP colleagues lost their jobs.
SESAR mints IGSN persistent identifiers for physical samples and is being redesigned to serve biodiversity samples.
Phase one of the IMLGS rescue recreated the portal as it was in January 2025 inside SESAR using GeoParquet; phase two will integrate the records into SESAR.
The ESIP Repository Crisis Scorecards (a Qualtrics survey on ESIP's site and Zenodo) assess preparedness for natural disaster, loss of funding, cyber attack and loss of personnel.
AGU's task groups work on business models, shared technical solutions, crisis preparedness kits and mutual aid agreements to take on one another's data.
datasets: Index to Marine and Lacustrine Geological Samples (IMLGS)

notable_claims.claim: Invisibility of infrastructure constitutes a passive threat to its ongoing existence.
Over 20 NOAA databases and data resources were taken offline following budget cuts in early 2025.
Half the people she used to work with at ESIP lost their jobs.

recommendations: Aim for prioritisation rather than perfection in preservation.
Work on advocacy to build political will and keep infrastructure appropriately visible.
Join the AGU resilience effort, which welcomes other domains.
future_work: SESAR phase two: integrate IMLGS records into the SESAR database with vocabulary changes.
examples_case_studies: SESAR rescue of NOAA's IMLGS portal.
ESIP Repository Crisis Scorecards.
AGU data resilience task groups.

representative_excerpt.text: To close, I'm struck by how all of these projects are about doing the best we can with what we have, or preparing to do the best we can with what we have.

notable_moments.description: Shift from passive to active threats to data infrastructure in the US.
The IMLGS data rescue into SESAR.
ESIP Repository Crisis Scorecards.
Prioritisation over perfection and a call for advocacy.

content_items.title: NEON, Community Standards, and the Hyper-Extended Specimen

programme.title: NEON, Community Standards, and the Hyper-Extended Specimen
programme.session: SYM38 Sustaining the Geo- and Biodiversity Data Ecosystem: Standards-Driven Approaches to Long-Term Resilience
programme.abstract:
Each year, the National Ecological Observatory Network (NEON) collects over 400 terabytes of ecological data and more than 100,000 spatially and temporally co-located geochemical samples and biological specimens across the United States. NEON monitors whole ecosystems through repeated field sampling, continuous sensor measurements, remote sensing, and downstream analyses, creating a unique opportunity to support “hyper-extended specimens” while minimizing common data challenges related to standardization.

NEON primarily maintains and publishes its data using internal data models, vocabularies and identifiers. However, many of NEON data conventions align with community standards, such as GBIF vocabularies, Darwin Core, IGSN IDs, Veg-X, MIxS, and USA-NPN phenophase definitions. Selected data are formally translated and republished through standards-based infrastructures such as GBIF, BOLD, AmeriFlux, and Google Earth Engine. In addition, we have explored how ecological monitoring datasets can be represented using emerging standards such as the Humboldt Extension and Darwin Core Data Package. We are also working with broader community efforts to examine and improve the AI readiness of our datasets to increase interoperability and relevance for next-generation analytical tools.

We outline the current state of the Digital Extended Specimen concept within the NEON ecosystem, including ongoing efforts and challenges to connect our physical collections, digital infrastructure, and diverse downstream research communities, while improving provenance tracking and discoverability.

actual.identification_notes: Speaker name rendered by ASR as 'Shandra Earl'; content matches the programme.

content_items.summary: Chandra Earl presented NEON's design for resilient, interoperable data and samples: 81 sites across 20 ecoclimatic domains, over 400 TB of data a year, and about 100,000 samples a year curated at the NEON Biorepository. She described provenance tracking, issue management, modular pipelines, digital-born sample data, DOIs/IGSNs and external audits, and showed small-mammal vouchers as a 'hyper-extended specimen' linking occurrences, images, tissues, traits, molecular and pathogen data. She closed with questions about citation and impact tracing, who sustains standards and crosswalks, getting commercial users to contribute, and round-tripping of value-added data.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: NEON was built for interoperability from the start, but sustaining standards, crosswalks and value-added links needs community-level solutions.
content_items.why_it_matters: NEON is a large, standards-aligned observatory whose hyper-extended specimens show both the power and the complexity of linked data, and its open questions set up the session discussion.
key_points: NEON is an NSF-funded, Battelle-operated observatory with 81 sites in 20 ecoclimatic domains, a planned 30-year lifespan and about seven years in.
It combines automated sensors, airborne remote sensing and observational sampling: over 400 TB a year, 650 million sensor readings a day and 2.5 PB stored.
Around 100,000 samples of about 65 types are archived yearly, representing over 8,000 taxa, mostly at the NEON Biorepository at Arizona State University.
Sample data are born digital (barcodes replaced handwritten labels) and accessioned samples receive DOIs for use tracking.
Data are audited for quality (Bob Mesibov) and AI readiness (ESIP).
NEON uses EML, Darwin Core, MIxS, ENVO, USA-NPN phenophases, IGSNs, dataset DOIs, ORCIDs and RORs, and is testing the Humboldt Extension and Darwin Core Data Package with GBIF.
NEON data are used beyond ecology: food security, drinking water safety after Hurricane Maria, permafrost pathogen sequencing and AI benchmark datasets.
questions: How can we ensure appropriate citation and ability to trace impact of shared data?
Who sustains standards, mappings and crosswalks as data and technologies evolve?
How do we encourage support from large or commercial entities who use the data?
How can downstream value-added data be made discoverable and connected (round-tripping)?

notable_claims.claim: NEON collects over 400 terabytes of data per year, with 650 million sensor readings per day and 2.5 petabytes stored in total.
NEON archives approximately 100,000 samples of about 65 sample types each year.

future_work: Test adoption of the Humboldt Extension and Darwin Core Data Package for NEON data.
examples_case_studies: Small mammal vouchers as hyper-extended specimens.
Alaska berry futures food security study.
Groundwater nitrate testing in Puerto Rico after Hurricane Maria.
Permafrost core pathogen sequencing with the US Department of Defense.

representative_excerpt.text: Standards improve interoperability, of course, but who sustains the standards? Who sustains the mappings? Who sustains the crosswalks as data and technologies evolve?

notable_moments.description: The hyper-extended specimen example of NEON small mammal vouchers.
Closing questions posed to the audience for discussion.

content_items.title: Canada’s need for synthesis for Adaptation and Resilience to Climate Change

programme.title: Canada’s need for synthesis for Adaptation and Resilience to Climate Change
programme.session: SYM38 Sustaining the Geo- and Biodiversity Data Ecosystem: Standards-Driven Approaches to Long-Term Resilience
programme.abstract:
The exponential growth of genomic data presents an unprecedented opportunity to mitigate the ecological impacts of climate change. Genomic data is estimated at 30 petabytes available publicly, with likely at least half as much unpublished. The Genomic Research and Development Initiative’s (GRDI) Genomic Adaptation and Resilience to Climate Change (GenARCC) will amass nearly a petabyte of data. Consequently, we may already have the raw genomic data required to address some of the most pressing ecological problems that can be solved using genomics.

To fully realize this potential, a paradigm shift towards systematic reuse of data and synthesis is essential. Synthesis centres have previously demonstrated the value of reanalyzing existing assets to accelerate discovery. This requires realigning incentives to prioritize data reuse over data generation such as by recognizing algorithms, associated pipelines and applications, and the data itself like long term scientific infrastructure. This involves standardization of data, processes, and products, which can only be realized by the community’s will and/or incentivized through funding-related obligations. With improved access and curation of shared scientific resources, researchers can develop novel data management architectures and leverage artificial intelligence, to integrate diverse datasets and reveal cross-system patterns of resilience that isolated studies overlook. To achieve this goal, future efforts should work towards FAIR data, and validation, maintenance, and automation of code and underlying algorithms. Together, these efforts can enhance how scientific data is shared and utilized in conservation and ecology. Prioritizing synthesis will ensure we get the highest return on our collective investment.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced as 'our own James Macklin'; content is on the GenARCC genomics project. Affiliation inferred from the Canadian federal context and DINA.

content_items.summary: James Macklin drew lessons from GenARCC, a large Canadian cross-departmental project using genomics to assess, predict and adapt to climate change, which will add about 20,000 whole genomes across 30 species largely from existing samples and specimens. He showed how the DINA research data management system captures standards-based metadata linked to material samples and sequences, and new pipelines push data semi-automatically to ENA and then associate ENA records with rich metadata in GBIF, compensating for poor metadata searchability in INSDC repositories. He stressed that relied-upon repositories carry funding risk, and that researchers undervalue the 'boring' work of connecting and standardising metadata needed for reuse and decision-ready results.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Genomic data can only support climate adaptation synthesis if metadata are captured with standards from the start and linked to discoverable infrastructures like GBIF.
content_items.why_it_matters: Environmental genomic data are growing rapidly, and the talk shows a practical pipeline (DINA to ENA to GBIF) for making sequence data findable while highlighting cultural barriers to reuse.
key_points: Public genomic data are estimated at 70+ petabytes; environmental metagenomics is a rapidly growing, highly diverse slice.
Canada has genome-level data for about 0.5% of its 80,000 species, biased toward economically and culturally important species.
GenARCC will add about 20,000 whole genomes across 30 terrestrial, marine and freshwater species, using existing samples via MTAs.
DINA captures a standards-based metadata snapshot with flexible managed attributes for terms not covered by standards.
About 740 salmon genomes were pushed from DINA to ENA via a semi-automatic pipeline.
INSDC repositories hold only core metadata searchably; a new workflow links ENA records to rich metadata in GBIF.
Researchers prioritise novel sequencing and analyses over metadata curation, reproducible code and reusable pipelines.

notable_claims.claim: GenARCC will add about 20,000 whole genomes across only 30 species.
Sequence repositories like SRA and ENA only make core metadata searchable; additional metadata are not FAIR.
Canada has genome-level data for about 0.5% of its 80,000 species.

recommendations: Manage data from the beginning with standards so it is reusable.
Researchers need to prioritise connecting and publishing metadata alongside genomic data.

programme.abstract:
To sustain a robust Geo-Biodiversity Data Ecosystem, SANBI has implemented standardised data management strategies for South Africa’s national botanical and zoological collections. The project focuses on transitioning legacy data into FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) datasets using globally recognised informatics standards. Central to this architecture is the National Biodiversity Information System (NBIS), which integrates data from institutional partners using standardised platforms.

A key challenge in national data integration is metadata harmonisation, particularly taxonomic inconsistencies. To address this, SANBI uses the TaxaMatch algorithm, which matches misspelt or variant species names to an authoritative taxonomic backbone. This ensures high-quality, interoperable data regardless of differing institutional interpretations. For botanical data, SANBI distributes authoritative dictionaries, including taxa with authors and gazetteer data, to improve quality at capture.

Institutions push new or updated data to staging instances where automated quality checks are applied before records move to production. ETL packages synchronise data regularly. For zoological collections, Specify’s taxonomic ranking system accommodates diverse research traditions while maintaining referential integrity.

The system supports spatial searches, enabling users to draw polygons on maps to retrieve species coordinates. SANBI also uses a separate NBIS indexing database with persistent identifiers linked across repositories. By providing shared infrastructure and standards, SANBI enables a scalable web portal that promotes data cleaning, reduces duplication, and supports environmental monitoring and research.

programme.title: FAIR ancient environmental DNA data in practice: developing and implementing interoperable metadata standards in AEGIS
programme.session: CO4 FAIR data in practice - eDNA, modelling and biodiversity concepts
programme.abstract: Ancient Environmental Genomics Initiative for Sustainability (AEGIS) is a seven-year programme investigating how records of adaptive responses stored in ancient environmental DNA (eDNA) coupled with other biomolecular approaches can support understanding of ecosystem resilience and sustainable food production, while preserving biodiversity, under climate change scenarios. The data engine, a core component of AEGIS, includes a strong commitment to FAIR and open data, with enriched metadata to promote findability, access, interoperability and re-use, with eDNA data shared via the European Nucleotide Archive (ENA) and other EMBL-EBI resources. To ensure FAIR, the team engaged with the Genomics Standards Consortium (GSC), which maintain metadata standards for eDNA under MIxS (Minimum Information for any Sequence), the community-led FAIRe (Making eDNA FAIR) project, and with the ancient DNA community working on MInAS (Minimum Information about any Ancient Sequence). The metadata collected under AEGIS was mapped to these existing and developing standards to construct metadata checklists and accurately describe experiment data in AEGIS. To facilitate compliance, AEGIS uses standardised metadata collection templates. This presentation will describe the implementation process, including the development of an ENA ancient DNA metadata checklist, approaches for capturing provenance and contextual metadata, and challenges in harmonising standards across biodiversity, eDNA, and ancient genomics domains. The work demonstrates how machine-readable and interoperable metadata standards can support scalable reuse of ancient eDNA data, improve reproducibility, and strengthen long-term integration of palaeogenomic resources into wider biodiversity and environmental data ecosystems.

content_items.title: Rethinking “absence” in biodiversity data collection and modeling

programme.title: Rethinking “absence” in biodiversity data collection and modeling
programme.session: CO4 FAIR data in practice - eDNA, modelling and biodiversity concepts
programme.abstract: The rapid growth of biodiversity data through GBIF and related sites has accelerated the development of species distribution models (SDMs) and occupancy models. Simultaneously, the literature has accumulated many partially overlapping terms related to “absence”, including absence record, confirmed absence, negative detection, zero count, and pseudo-absence. A working group with experience in biodiversity data collection, curation, and modeling met monthly for approximately 18 months to sort out this confusing terminology. Most biodiversity sampling compendia did not explicitly define absence-related terms. When they did, usage varied: some sources used presence-absence language, whereas others used detection-non-detection language. The occupancy-modeling literature provided a stronger conceptual framework for data collection (MacKenzie (2005). Here detection and non-detection characterize observations, whereas presence and absence are inferred ecological states that can be estimated probabilistically with repeated survey data. This perspective motivated a petition, introduced by members of our working group and others, to change the values of occurrenceStatus in the Humboldt Extension from “present/absent” to “detected/nonDetected.” SDMs use another set of absence-related terms, such as pseudo-absence, presence-pseudoabsence data, and true absence. For modeling, ordinary language is insufficient. These terms have technical meanings that depend on model class, data type, sampling assumptions, and historical context. During this innovative phase of model development, it seems difficult to create standardized terminology, MacKenzie, D. I. 2005. What are the issues with presence-absence data for wildlife managers? Journal of Wildlife Management 69: 849-860.

content_items.summary: Rob Stevenson presented the outcome of a working group (with Abby Benson, Ruben Perez, Deborah Arlt, Yiming and Wesley Hochachka) on confusing 'absence' terminology. He argued presence and absence are asymmetric (presence is a fact, absence a question) and absence is only meaningful against an expectation frame such as a Humboldt Extension survey target. Surveying methodology and analysis texts, the group found the museum (presence-only) and biological survey (repeated, effort-based) communities use different data and models, with detectability as the unifying concept. The main outcome was the TDWG Executive's approval in May of changing Darwin Core occurrenceStatus values from present/absent to detected/not detected.

Detectability, from mark-recapture, distance sampling and occupancy models, is the key clarifying concept.

content_items.title: Challenges and Opportunities for FAIR Marine eDNA Data Publication Workflows

programme.title: Challenges and Opportunities for FAIR Marine eDNA Data Publication Workflows
programme.session: CO4 FAIR data in practice - eDNA, modelling and biodiversity concepts
programme.abstract:
Marine environmental DNA (eDNA) dataset volumes are increasing rapidly as eDNA becomes integrated into routine sampling workflows on research vessels and in monitoring programs. However, challenges related to interoperability, metadata standardisation, and repository integration remain and require further work to support future interoperable biodiversity data infrastructure and FAIR data publication workflows.

In this project, we aim to assess current challenges and community needs associated with marine eDNA data publication and interoperability.

We are designing evaluation instruments to assess the current landscape of marine eDNA data publication workflows. We are reviewing existing workflows, tools, metadata standards, and FAIR requirements associated with biodiversity publication pathways. Through surveys and consultations with key stakeholders, we are mapping workflows from sample collection through to data mobilisation and publication. Stakeholder engagement has included collaboration and discussions with Australian and international biodiversity organisations, data infrastructure initiatives, and sequencing and biodiversity data communities.

Preliminary findings indicate that there is a strong interest within the eDNA community in publishing and reusing biodiversity data. However, results suggest inconsistent adoption of metadata standards, fragmented publication workflows, time-consuming publication processes, and incomplete metadata collection practices that may reduce FAIR compliance and data reusability.

This work will inform approaches to interoperable infrastructure for marine eDNA data publication and support FAIR adoption, thereby increasing reusability of marine biodiversity datasets.

content_items.title: Visualising specimens as event chains on the Australian Reference Genome Atlas

programme.title: Visualising specimens as event chains on the Australian Reference Genome Atlas
programme.session: CO4 FAIR data in practice - eDNA, modelling and biodiversity concepts
programme.abstract: The Australian Reference Genome Atlas (ARGA) was built in partnership by the Atlas of Living Australia, Australian BioCommons, and Bioplatforms Australia to index whole genome sequence data from Australian biodiversity species and other eukaryote species relevant to Australia’s needs for the bioinformatics community. As part of the project, we created a new model for tracking the provenance of genomic data, tracing specimens from their wild state through to laboratory processing, and appending data objects to their relevant source samples. Here, we outline the data requirements, the selection of fields, and the backend database structure used to facilitate the provenance chain from specimen to data object. We developed a dynamic and extensible demonstration UI, supported by these fields and architecture, to guide users through a discovery journey within the specimen area of the ARGA interface. Using an example, we will demonstrate how users can navigate from a specimen or tissue to a genomic data packet to reveal collection information, protocols, and agents for a rich provenance history display. Underpinning a card-based interface was the aim of ARGA to facilitate deeper ways of exploring and interacting with data for the genomics user community. The ARGA project has now concluded, and we aim to extract lessons and components that we can reuse within the Atlas of Living Australia (https://www.ala.org.au) and which may be repurposed by other platforms that share DNA-derived biodiversity data. We will explore the applicability of this component within other collections-based online interfaces, such as for museums collections and biobanks.

content_items.summary: Kathryn Hall described how the Australian Reference Genome Atlas (ARGA), an index rather than repository, modelled provenance chains from a wild organism through collection, museum registration, tissue subsampling, DNA extraction and lab runs to deposited genomic data products. The result lets users see, for example, 31 derived data products from one specimen with tissue, molecule, file type and custodian preserved.

content_items.title: Bridging Biodiversity Data Standards and Predictive Ecology: Operationalizing Interoperable Workflows for Species Distribution Modeling in West Africa

programme.title: Bridging Biodiversity Data Standards and Predictive Ecology: Operationalizing Interoperable Workflows for Species Distribution Modeling in West Africa
programme.session: CO4 FAIR data in practice - eDNA, modelling and biodiversity concepts
programme.abstract: Biodiversity data standards have enabled large-scale aggregation of species occurrence records, yet their translation into reproducible analytical workflows remains uneven, particularly in data-limited regions. This study operationalizes standardized biodiversity data for machine learning-based species distribution modeling, using threatened tropical timber species in West Africa as a case study. We develop an interoperable workflow integrating species occurrence records structured with Darwin Core and high-resolution bioclimatic variables. The approach emphasizes data harmonization, metadata completeness, and spatial validation to address challenges such as sampling bias, coordinate uncertainty, and inconsistent taxonomy. By aligning heterogeneous datasets within a standards-compliant framework, the workflow supports reproducible and reusable analyses. Preliminary results suggest that adherence to biodiversity data standards improves model robustness and transparency, particularly in underrepresented regions. Predicted distributions under current and future climate scenarios highlight both suitable habitats and areas where data limitations affect model reliability. This work extends the role of biodiversity data standards from data mobilization to fully integrated analytical pipelines. By linking standards-based data management with predictive ecology, it demonstrates how interoperable workflows can enhance biodiversity data use for conservation decision-making and global assessments, especially in data-sparse regions such as West Africa.

actual.identification_notes: Pre-recorded video; name transcribed as 'Peter Ogheghe'. Title and content match the programme.

content_items.summary: Peter Ugege reported a controlled experiment asking whether standards-informed processing of occurrence records changes species distribution model outcomes for six West African timber species. Starting from 46,941 records, the standards pathway removed 106 records (placeholders, duplicates, a fuzzy and absent records), but after domain restriction and spatial deduplication both pathways converged on identical 36,407 presence units, so no pathway-specific predictive effect was identifiable. Geographic cross-validation gave ROC-AUC of about 0.66-0.75, far below random cross-validation (~0.99), showing random validation overstates transferability.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Standards change what enters a modelling pipeline, but workflow design determines whether that difference survives and validation design determines what claims can be made.
content_items.why_it_matters: It gives a rigorous, reproducible test of the downstream effect of data standards on SDMs and a clear warning about optimistic random cross-validation.
key_points: Three levels of effect were distinguished: record representation, numerical SDM information and predictive inference.
Pathway A (minimal processing) kept 46,941 records; pathway B (standards-informed fitness-for-use rules) kept 46,835, a 0.23% difference.
Within the West African domain the difference fell to 70 records, concentrated in three species and 16 locations, all already represented in pathway B.
After common spatial deduplication both yielded 36,407 presence units and the same 96,407-row modelling matrix.
Models: logistic regression, random forest and histogram gradient boosting, with strict geographic cross-validation.
Random CV mean ROC-AUC ~0.99 vs ~0.70 under geographic hold-out (mean difference 0.28).
No species was best on every robustness dimension, so no composite score was used.
datasets: Occurrence records for six West African timber species (46,941 records)

notable_claims.claim: Both pathways converged on exactly 36,407 presence sampling units after common spatial deduplication.
Random cross-validation gave mean ROC-AUC about 0.99 versus about 0.70 under geographic hold-out.

recommendations: Make standards, workflow decisions and validation design explicit for reproducible modelling.
Use geographic rather than random cross-validation when transferability matters.
results_findings: Standards-informed processing produced a measurable record-level effect (106 records, 0.23%).
The difference did not survive common spatial processing, so no pathway-specific predictive effect was identifiable.

programme.title: The future is the future - thought about access to data in publications
programme.session: SYM45 Planning the Libroscope: creating research ready biodiversity from scientific publications
programme.abstract:
Scientific publications contain a large share of humanity’s knowledge on biodiversity and are becoming increasingly important as training and reference sources for Artificial Intelligence applications. Yet most biodiversity literature remains difficult for machines to access and interpret. Estimates suggest a corpus of hundreds of millions of printed pages, with 50,000-200,000 biodiversity-related articles and around 2,000 taxonomy-relevant journals published annually. Resources such as the Biodiversity Heritage Library and Plazi demonstrate both the scale of the challenge and the feasibility of extracting structured biodiversity knowledge from publications.

Biodiversity publications not only describe taxa and synthesize research, but also cite specimens, observations and datasets, thereby linking natural science collections, occurrence records and scientific interpretations. However, most publications are still produced primarily for human reading and lack machine-actionable semantic structure. Unlocking this knowledge at scale therefore requires strategic prioritisation.

Within the framework of the Disentis Roadmap, which aims to liberate biodiversity knowledge from the literature by 2034, key questions arise: should limited resources focus on continued digitisation of historical print literature, semantic enhancement of legacy publications, or the promotion of future-ready publishing workflows that produce structured and FAIR-compliant data from the outset, as demonstrated by initiatives such as Pensoft and CETAF?

This contribution argues that a practical compromise is the development of a Biodiversity Libroscope: a framework to systematically digitise, extract and publish semantically standardised biodiversity knowledge from well-defined corpora of literature.

programme.title: Realtime Access to Data in new Taxonomic Publications
programme.session: SYM45 Planning the Libroscope: creating research ready biodiversity from scientific publications
programme.abstract:
Taxonomic knowledge is published at an accelerating rate across hundreds of journals, creating major challenges for aggregators and biodiversity databases to keep up. Many articles are available only as PDFs, lack machine-actionable structure, and are often hidden behind paywalls, making automated extraction of taxonomic names, type specimens, and diagnostic data increasingly difficult.

This work presents Plazi's semantics-aware, modular workflow that converts in realtime taxonomic publications published as PDFs or XML into open, FAIR, and machine-actionable biodiversity data and semantically enhanced articles. Structured PDFs are decoded to infer document structure, while XML publications (e.g. JATS-TaxPub) are processed directly through embedded semantic markup. Publication streams are harvested through RSS feeds or direct ingestion as part of editorial workflows.

Extracted taxonomic treatments, figures, tables, materials citations, and bibliographic data are semantically enhanced and linked to external repositories and taxonomic reference systems. Automated quality control is complemented by targeted manual correction where required. Outputs are disseminated in near real time through standards-based formats including DwCA, ColDP, and JATS-TaxPub XML. TreatmentBank currently contributes more than 58,000 datasets to the Global Biodiversity Information Facility, over 80,000 new species records to GBIF and the Catalogue of Life, more than one million treatments to BiodiversityPMC, and 800,000 figures as FAIR digital objects in the Biodiversity Literature Repository.

programme.session: SYM45 Planning the Libroscope: creating research ready biodiversity from scientific publications
programme.abstract:
Since the earliest observations of the living world, scientific literature has been the primary medium for documenting and disseminating biodiversity knowledge. Over centuries, this process has generated a vast corpus of taxonomic, ecological, biogeographic, and recently also molecular information. Yet, much of these data remain embedded in PDF-based publications, limiting their findability, accessibility, interoperability, and computational reuse.

Although data extraction and annotation tools have been produced to address this issue and unlock biodiversity data from PDFs, it is crucial to stop extending the legacy backlog. According to the Disentis vision, this presentation proposes to shift toward semantically enhanced publishing workflows designed to readily produce FAIR, interlinked, and AI-ready data, a process that started more than a decade ago as part of the ViBRANT FP7 project and was subsequently carried out successfully through the pro-iBiosphere, EU BON, and BiCIKL projects.

XML-first workflows for prospective literature (MetoTaxa, ARPHA) will be presented from semantic markup to enrichment and publication through interconnected infrastructures. Particular emphasis will be placed on the standards (e.g., JATS-TaxPub), vocabularies (e.g., Darwin Core), and resolvable persistent identifiers.

By supporting large-scale knowledge integration and machine-actionable biodiversity data, such workflows create new opportunities for emerging AI applications and also improve support for many other machine driven forms of reuse.

content_items.title: Building digital-native species: Transitioning from PDF liberation to semantic-by-design publishing

programme.title: Building digital-native species: Transitioning from PDF liberation to semantic-by-design publishing
programme.session: SYM45 Planning the Libroscope: creating research ready biodiversity from scientific publications
programme.abstract:
Scientific publications remain the primary vehicle for communicating biodiversity knowledge. The Bouchout Declaration marked an important step toward opening biodiversity literature and mobilising the taxonomic knowledge embedded within publications. Since then, major efforts have focused on liberating biodiversity data from legacy PDFs through text mining, semantic annotation and automated extraction workflows, enabling large-scale mobilisation of taxonomic names, treatments and material citations.

However, PDF-centric approaches remain limited by the publication format itself. Extracting structured knowledge from PDFs is retrospective, heterogeneous and costly, often requiring complex workflows to recover semantics that were never encoded during publication.

In the framework of the Disentis Roadmap and the Biodiversity Libroscope initiative, this contribution argues for a transition from retrospective data liberation to digital-first and XML-first publishing workflows that generate machine-actionable biodiversity knowledge by design. Central to this vision is the concept of “digital-native species”, in which species descriptions and supporting evidence are created, published and maintained in interoperable semantic environments from the outset.

Publications remain the formal scholarly record but are generated from, and linked to, structured specimen-level evidence including images, sequences, measurements, treatments and collection records. Semantic XML publishing enables fine-grained markup, interoperability across infrastructures and direct integration with natural science collections and global biodiversity platforms.

This contribution discusses how semantic-by-design publishing can create interconnected, computable and AI-ready biodiversity knowledge ecosystems.

programme.title: Literature triage to support Island Biodiversity Monitoring
programme.session: SYM45 Planning the Libroscope: creating research ready biodiversity from scientific publications
programme.abstract:
Biodiversity research increasingly relies on vast quantities of scientific literature, therefore developing screening tools to better scan the literature is essential. Island biodiversity was selected as a test bed thanks to the support of Biodiversa+. An automatic triage system was developed and applied to Biodiversity Island monitoring.

We started by querying OpenAlex with broad coverage Boolean equations. Further, a binary classifier for island ecosystem publications (BioMoQA project) was developed using pre-trained bidirectional language models. After manual selection, the articles are then indexed into SIBiLS/BiodiversityPMC (https://biodiversitypmc.sibils.org/). Using 5-fold cross-validation on 1,434 abstracts, we compared domain-specific biomedical transformers (e.g., BioBERT, BiomedBERT) for life sciences against general-purpose models (e.g., BERT, RoBERTa), which are combined with ensemble learning. Binary cross-entropy ensembles achieved best performance with ROC-AUC of 0.926. The reported model performance is competitive with curator inter-rater agreement (expert kappa ~0.78). The classifier is now integrated in the SIBiLS\BiodiversityPMC platform, and through weekly screening ensures consistent up to date coverage of island biodiversity literature, thus supporting the harmonization of global island biodiversity monitoring efforts. The service platform is currently being applied to other biodiversity assessment projects and could likely serve a large set of biodiversity communities.

programme.session: SYM45 Planning the Libroscope: creating research ready biodiversity from scientific publications
programme.abstract:
The Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES) produces global assessments that rely heavily on scientific literature as a primary source of evidence. Over time, the literature search practices within IPBES have evolved considerably - from reliance on closed, proprietary databases such as Web of Science and Scopus, toward open infrastructure like OpenAlex combined with scripted, reproducible, and transparent search strategies.

This talk traces that evolution and reflects on what has been learned along the way. It examines the trade-offs between different database choices, the shift toward programmatic and auditable search workflows, and the persistent challenge that scientific publications - while rich in factual biodiversity data - remain written for human consumption and are rarely machine-actionable.

A further complication is the role of grey literature - reports, technical documents, government publications, and other non-peer-reviewed sources that contain an abundance of important information and knowledge, yet remain largely invisible to standard bibliographic infrastructure. Grey literature is at best inconsistently indexed, poorly structured, and often inaccessible at scale, making systematic discovery and extraction particularly difficult.

Looking forward, I discuss how the Libroscope vision addresses the machine-actionability gap: by systematically liberating, structuring, and connecting biodiversity knowledge from the published literature in FAIR-compliant, AI-ready formats. The IPBES experience provides a concrete use case illustrating both the current limitations and the transformative potential that a shared Libroscope instrument could deliver for evidence-based biodiversity policy.

Combining biodiversity genomics and AI-driven text mining has the potential to transform how biodiversity data are integrated for species and habitat protection and restoration. The project’s central focus is the large-scale extraction of species traits from biodiversity and taxonomic literature to improve integrative species distribution and taxonomic richness modelling. It aims to deliver an open-access knowledge graph and modelling portal linking text-mined traits, genomic indicators, and environmental layers for transparent, reusable analyses.

Current species distribution models increasingly incorporate traits and genomic data, but progress is limited by difficulties accessing and harmonising heterogeneous data sources. We will address this through AI-assisted literature digitisation, named-entity recognition and normalisation, relationship extraction, and semi-automated expert curation to convert biodiversity literature into machine-actionable trait datasets. These text-mined traits will be integrated with genomic analyses and benchmarked against occurrence-only models to quantify gains in predictive power and ecological realism.

The project is also addressing uncertainties from incomplete taxonomy and undescribed “dark taxa” through taxonomic reconciliation and uncertainty propagation within modelling workflows. Research focuses on birds, bats, and fish in Switzerland, and butterflies, bumblebees, and amphipods across Europe, providing case studies for evaluating literature-mining approaches. Resulting workflows and decision-ready maps will support biodiversity research and conservation planning in Switzerland and across Europe.

content_items.title: Mapping geographical distributions in the World Register of Marine Species

programme.title: Mapping geographical distributions in the World Register of Marine Species
programme.session: SYM26 From WDSRPD to GeoSchemes: Recording Biodiversity Distributions for Science and Policy
programme.abstract:
The World Register of Marine Species (WoRMS) is an authoritative database hosted at the Flanders Marine Institute (VLIZ), aiming to provide a comprehensive list of all marine organisms. Associated information on the species includes “Documented distribution” backed by published sources. Since the beginnings of WoRMS this representation has been hampered by the lack of an agreed set of geounits, of homogeneous extension. For this reason the Geoschemes task group of TDWG was set up to undertake a proposal, which will parallel the current “World Geographic Scheme for Recording Plant Distribution” used on land.

Purposes of this set of geounits is twofold: (1) to provide a sensible visual representation of a species’ range, aso able to handle imprecise country-level records from the old literature and (2) to provide bounding boxes for the retrieval of distribution data and species lists, particularly at the country level.

The countries’ Exclusive Economic Zones (EEZs) were either taken as recording units or subdivided where needed, and the High Seas were subdivided according to physiographical features in the bathyal and abyssal stages respectively. A hierarchical set of five Level-1 units, 26 Level-2 units, 232 Level-3 units and 536 Level-4 units is currently under review. Subdivision of the large or complex EEZs followed Marine Ecoregions of the World or the IHO Limits of Oceans and Seas when appropriate, and existing local schemes were adopted for Europe and Australia. Attempts to distinguish habitats were disregarded in view of the advantages of having a standard representation for all the species: therefore, representing a polygon as a distribution record assumes that the species exists “somewhere” inside, not everywhere.

content_items.summary: Serge Gofas explained why WoRMS needed a standard set of marine geounits: species distributions were recorded with haphazard units. Neither EEZs (too uneven) nor Marine Ecoregions of the World (ignoring borders) were adequate, so the TDWG GeoSchemes marine task group published a hierarchical proposal with five oceans, ~200 level-two and 577 level-four units, coastal areas split country-wise and high seas based on Watling et al. He raised the unresolved issue of how to write English 'definitions' required by the TDWG standards specification for spatial units, proposing reference to maps in Marine Regions, and outlined uses including national checklists, cross-checking GBIF/OBIS points and global analysis.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: A country-aware, hierarchical marine geoscheme will let WoRMS and others record and query distributions consistently, pending a solution for defining spatial units in a TDWG standard.
content_items.why_it_matters: It extends a widely used TDWG geographic standard to the oceans, enabling national marine checklists and literature-based distribution records.
key_points: WoRMS is curated by 300+ experts and hosted at VLIZ; its distribution tab suffered from inconsistent geounits.
EEZs work for small countries but large or multi-coast countries need subdivision.
MEOW ignores country borders, making locality assignment ambiguous.
Level one: major oceans; level two: coastal areas by biogeographic region plus high seas; level four: 577 units.
High seas use Watling et al. with a 3,500 m threshold between bathyal and abyssal.
Unit codes are unique across terrestrial and marine parts and can serve as controlled vocabulary strings.
Unit sizes (100,000-500,000 km2) are comparable to five-degree grids.

content_items.title: Marine Regions as a backbone for the TDWG Marine GeoScheme

programme.title: Marine Regions as a backbone for the TDWG Marine GeoScheme
programme.session: SYM26 From WDSRPD to GeoSchemes: Recording Biodiversity Distributions for Science and Policy
programme.abstract:
Marine Regions provides a standard of marine georeferenced locations, boundaries and regions for scientific and educational purposes. At its core is a hierarchical gazetteer that serves as a geographic backbone for a wide range of applications, from biodiversity infrastructures such as the World Register of Marine Species (WoRMS), to global fisheries initiatives such as Global Fishing Watch.

Beyond place names and boundaries, Marine Regions brings together diverse geospatial ecological classifications relevant to the recording and interpretation of marine biodiversity distributions. These include global and regional frameworks, such as the Marine Ecoregions of the World (MEOW), Longhurst provinces, DFO Marine Bioregions and IMCRA Provincial Bioregions. In addition, it develops and maintains data products that are important for distribution recording, but are not always readily available or consistently managed elsewhere, including maritime boundaries such as Exclusive Economic Zones (EEZ). Marine Regions has also integrated the TDWG Terrestrial Scheme since 2015.

This experience positions Marine Regions as an active contributor to the development of the proposed TDWG Marine GeoScheme within the broader GeoSchemes framework. Its contribution is twofold: providing relevant source data, including Exclusive Economic Zones and IHO Sea Areas, and contributing technical expertise on how to build, version and maintain such a standard in a consistent and sustainable way. Once finalised, the TDWG Marine GeoScheme will be integrated into Marine Regions, where its areas will receive persistent unique identifiers (PIDs), Marine Regions Geographic Identifiers (MRGIDs), enabling stable, unambiguous citation, machine to machine linkage, and use in (biodiversity) data publication.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced as Brit; name transcribed as 'Brit Lonnewele'.

content_items.summary: Britt Lonneville introduced Marine Regions as the backbone for the marine geoscheme: a gazetteer of nearly 65,000 marine places with persistent MRGIDs, taken from authoritative sources and hierarchically related, openly licensed maritime boundary datasets digitised from UNCLOS legislation, and other geospatial layers such as IHO S-23 sea areas and MEOW. Marine Regions provides base data to the task group, works on development and standardisation with WoRMS, and will host and maintain the resulting units.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Marine Regions supplies the identifiers, boundaries and hierarchy that make a marine geoscheme maintainable.
content_items.why_it_matters: A persistent, maintained gazetteer is what makes geographic standards usable and updatable over time.
key_points: Three pillars: a gazetteer, open maritime boundary datasets, and relevant geospatial layers.
The gazetteer is the geographic counterpart to WoRMS, with nearly 65,000 features and MRGID identifiers.
Names come from authoritative sources (WGSRPD, MEOW, GEBCO, national gazetteers), mapped to one identifier.
Parent-child relations allow hierarchies, including alternative parents.
EEZs and other UNCLOS zones are digitised from legislation under CC BY and updated for new legislation, rulings and feedback.
Final GeoScheme units will be added to the gazetteer and available for download.

notable_claims.claim: The Marine Regions gazetteer has almost 65,000 features.

future_work: Add GeoScheme units to the Marine Regions gazetteer.

q_and_a.answer_summary: A French Mediterranean EEZ unit can have both France and the Mediterranean as parents, so either query retrieves it.

content_items.title: The new World Geographical Scheme for Recording (not only) Plant Distributions: process, progress and challenges

programme.title: The new World Geographical Scheme for Recording (not only) Plant Distributions: process, progress and challenges
programme.session: SYM26 From WDSRPD to GeoSchemes: Recording Biodiversity Distributions for Science and Policy
programme.abstract:
The World Geographical Scheme for Recording Plant Distributions (WGSRPD) has been one of the most widely used TDWG standards, supporting biodiversity data management, floristic synthesis, conservation assessments and scientific publishing for more than two decades. Its combination of administrative boundaries and biogeographical concepts within a hierarchical geographical framework proved both practical and broadly interoperable.

However, the current version of WGSRPD, published in 2001, requires substantial revision to remain relevant and useful. Changes in political boundaries, evolving community practices, the emergence of global biodiversity infrastructures, and new expectations regarding interoperability, transparency and machine-actionability all demand an updated approach.

The TDWG GeoSchemes Task Group is developing a new framework intended to extend and modernize WGSRPD beyond its original plant-focused scope. The work aims to preserve compatibility with the conceptual strengths of WGSRPD while introducing clearer governance, persistent identifiers, explicit versioning, improved documentation, and alignment with contemporary biodiversity data standards and policy needs.

This presentation will provide an overview of the principles guiding the revision process, the structure and intended outputs of the new GeoSchemes framework, current progress of the terrestrial domain work, and some of the main conceptual and technical challenges being addressed. It will also outline remaining work and opportunities for community participation and review.

actual.identification_notes: Speaker self-identifies as Paco Pando, convener of the terrestrial task group.

content_items.summary: Paco Pando described updating the WGSRPD, conceived by Dick Brummitt as a politically neutral, four-level scheme following political borders with phytogeographic sense. The terrestrial task group reviewed changes since 2001, now referencing UN naming conventions and precise polygons (prepared by the Pl@ntNet team from OpenStreetMap coastlines) rather than the Times Atlas; about 50 changes were needed and 34 issues resolved, yielding 9, 52, 369 and 617 units at levels one to four. Remaining meta-issues include one or two standards, where polygons live (Marine Regions, Zenodo), the name (GeoSchemes?) and open polygon formats (GeoJSON, FlatGeobuf).
content_items.one_line_takeaway: The terrestrial update is complete and the standard is nearly ready for public review, with packaging, naming and polygon hosting still to decide.
content_items.why_it_matters: WGSRPD is the most widely used TDWG standard after Darwin Core, so its modernisation and extension to all taxa affects many databases.
key_points: WGSRPD is used by Plants of the World, IUCN, USDA GRIN and cited 300+ times since 2022.
It is not a biogeographic standard; that role is played by the older Takhtajan floristic regions standard.
The Interest Group (2021) has two task groups: terrestrial update and new marine scheme, coordinated to avoid duplicate identifiers.
References move from the Times Atlas to UN naming conventions and the UN country names database; definitions become actual polygons.
Around 50 changes in names or borders; 34 issues resolved; terrestrial work considered complete.
Next: publish tables as CSV, public review, ratification; also a crosswalk from the old version and guidance.
questions: Should terrestrial and marine domains be one standard or two?
Should the standard be renamed (e.g. GeoSchemes)?
Which open polygon format should be used?

notable_claims.claim: The updated terrestrial scheme has 9 level-one, 52 level-two, 369 level-three and 617 level-four units.
Since 2022 the scheme has received over 300 citations in scientific publications.

results_findings: About 50 changes were needed; 34 issues resolved; terrestrial work complete.
future_work: Public review and ratification of the updated standard.

q_and_a.answer_summary: Pando agreed on one normative source propagated elsewhere.

q_and_a.question: How are legitimately disputed territories decided?
q_and_a.answer_summary: Following the UN position, e.g. Crimea's ISO code goes to Ukraine; Crimea is also a botanical unit.

q_and_a.answer_summary: Pierre Bonnet answered that OpenStreetMap coastlines were clipped.

content_items.title: Digitising Plant and Fungal Collections at Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew: Applying International Standards to Support Data Sharing and Geospatial Analysis

programme.title: Digitising Plant and Fungal Collections at Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew: Applying International Standards to Support Data Sharing and Geospatial Analysis
programme.session: SYM26 From WDSRPD to GeoSchemes: Recording Biodiversity Distributions for Science and Policy
programme.abstract: RBG, Kew holds over 8 M plant and fungal materials across 12 diverse collections and recently completed a major collection-based initiative to create a comprehensive digital catalogue, implement an Integrated Collections Management System (ICMS), and launch the Kew Data Portal. ICMS enhances data standardisation, curation, accessibility, and interoperability, enabling a strategic opportunity for integrated analysis across collections within a single digital platform. We present our experience in application of WGSRPD standards. Data derive from migrated legacy databases with varying standards, as well as entry of new records. A semi-automated process assigns TDWG levels based on ISO 3166 country codes for original provenance. ICMS currently holds over 7.8 M records linked to physical materials. While some materials are of historical significance dating back to BCE, collection events from original localities range from the late 17th century, with the most from the 19 th century onward. Over 1.44 M records could not be assigned to a country or territory without further investigation, while a high proportion met international data standards: ISO codes - 81.3%; TDWG L1 - 80.4%, L2 - 71.6%, L3 - 53.1%, and L4 - 52.9%. Provenance spans all 249 countries and territories, mainly from Africa, followed by Asia-Tropical and Southern America. Key challenges include missing hierarchical locality data, historical references, geopolitical boundary changes, transcontinental nations, multi-jurisdictional archipelagos, absent geocoordinates, language and translation inconsistencies, and variable user familiarity with the TDWG system. Our results highlight both the value and the limitations of applying contemporary standards to heterogeneous, historically complex biodiversity data.

actual.identification_notes: Speaker self-identifies (transcribed 'Udhyangani Liyum').

content_items.summary: Udayangani Liu presented how Kew applied WGSRPD in its Integrated Collections Management System after a four-year mass digitisation that imaged over six million herbarium and fungarium specimens. Selecting an ISO country semi-automatically populates TDWG levels, while transcontinental countries, multi-country archipelagos and changed boundaries need level-by-level handling. Analysis of 7.9 million records spanning five centuries showed ISO codes are well captured but only just over 50% have levels three and four, with about 1.5 million records lacking a continent; challenges include historical data, missing hierarchy, language and variable user familiarity with the scheme.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: WGSRPD enables cross-collection geospatial analysis at Kew, but historical, heterogeneous data leave half of records without fine-level assignment.
content_items.why_it_matters: It is a real-world large-scale application of the standard being revised, surfacing practical issues the new version must accommodate.
key_points: Kew holds over 8 million items across 12 collections; ICMS manages them in one system following TDWG, Darwin Core and other protocols.
Over six million records were added in the mass digitisation project.
Choosing an ISO country auto-populates TDWG levels; large countries require state/province choice.
About 70% of records capture collecting year; dates span five centuries with dips during the World Wars.
Just over 50% of records capture TDWG levels three and four; ~1.5 million (20%) lack continent.
Data shared via Kew Data Portal, GBIF, DiSSCo UK, Genesys and the Svalbard Seed Vault.

notable_claims.claim: ICMS holds over 7.9 million digital records attached to physical objects.
Just over 50% of records capture TDWG levels three and four.
About 1.5 million records (20%) have no known continent.

limitations: Variable user familiarity with the TDWG scheme.
Transcontinental countries and archipelagos need detailed georeferencing.
future_work: Further georeferencing to assign missing levels.
examples_case_studies: A wreath of leaves dated to 1 BC collected in 1888.

q_and_a.answer_summary: Some records have localities needing detailed georeferencing (e.g. transcontinental countries); the four-year project prioritised speed.
